title: Poorly regenerative anaemia, pancytopenia and marrow disorders
definition: In canine babesiosis, the marrow problem is usually not marrow failure. It is an inadequate regenerative response: a low absolute reticulocyte count (ARC) for the degree of anaemia, with a hypercellular, dysplastic marrow [R1][R2]. Pancytopenia at presentation is common in B. canis and B. gibsoni and is mostly transient [R6][R9]. True marrow hypoplasia and haemophagocytic syndrome are rare and point to a co-infection or another cause [R10][R15].
definition_note: Changed. The working definition (non-regenerative anaemia, pancytopenia or haemophagocytic syndrome) implied marrow failure. The only marrow study in B. rossi found a hypercellular marrow with ineffective erythropoiesis, not hypoplasia [R1]. No study found an aplastic marrow caused by Babesia alone. The page title was changed from 'Bone marrow failure' to match; the coordinator may restore it in index.json.
key_points: A low ARC at presentation is expected: in B. rossi the ARC was not regenerative on day 0 and day 1 and rose by day 3 after diminazene [R3].
Do not call the anaemia non-regenerative before about 4 to 8 days of anaemia; regeneration needs that long to show [R1].
Automated analysers can count parasitised red cells as reticulocytes; check a manual count with new methylene blue on the smear [R13].
Pancytopenia was found in about 40 to 54% of dogs with acute B. canis and resolved with antibabesial treatment in most of them [R6][R7][R8].
Cytopenias that persist after effective treatment need a search for E. canis or Theileria, and a bone marrow aspirate and core biopsy [R15][R16].
Darbepoetin gave no benefit in B. gibsoni [R18]. Filgrastim and N-acetylcysteine were reported to help in small Indian studies, but the evidence is weak [R9][R20].

description.heading: What it is
description.text: Three different findings are grouped here. First, an inadequately regenerative anaemia: the ARC is too low for the haematocrit, although the marrow is active [R1][R2]. Second, bicytopenia or pancytopenia in the blood at presentation, mainly in B. canis and B. gibsoni [R6][R9]. Third, rare marrow disorders: haemophagocytic syndrome [R10], or marrow hypoplasia or myelofibrosis from a co-infection or a different piroplasm [R15][R16].

description.heading: How common, and in which dogs
description.text: In 103 dogs with B. rossi, the median ARC at presentation was 82 x10^9/L at a median haematocrit of 0.16 L/L (16%), lower than in dogs with IMHA at a similar haematocrit [R2]. In B. canis in Germany, pancytopenia was found in 19 of 46 dogs (41%) [R6], 135 of 342 dogs (39%) [R7] and 44 of 81 dogs (54%) [R8]. In one Indian referral clinic, 54 of 120 dogs with babesiosis were pancytopenic; the study dogs had B. gibsoni [R9]. Co-infection with E. canis was found in only 3 of 149 dogs with B. rossi in the Eastern Cape [R14].

description.heading: When in the course of disease
description.text: In experimental B. rossi, the ARC fell about 48 h after parasites appeared and rose after treatment [R2]. In natural B. rossi, the ARC was not regenerative on day 0 and day 1, moderately regenerative on day 3 and mildly regenerative on day 6 [R3]. In B. canis, the ARC was below 65 x10^9/L at admission and high 14 days after imidocarb [R4]. In another B. canis study, leukopenia resolved by about day 15 in 8 of 13 dogs, and 6 of 19 anaemic dogs had no reticulocytosis at day 15 or day 32 [R5].

description.heading: Mechanism
description.text: In fatal B. rossi, the marrow was hypercellular, with erythroid and myeloid hyperplasia, dysplastic metarubricytes, more macrophages with erythrophagocytosis and abundant stored iron [R1]. The authors conclude that dyserythropoiesis and inflammation, not a lack of iron or of marrow cells, explain the poor response [R1]. In vitro, serum from dogs with B. gibsoni delayed reticulocyte maturation [R17]. Serum erythropoietin was raised in most dogs with babesiosis in one study [R19]. Megakaryocytes were normal or increased, so the thrombocytopenia is peripheral [R1].

species_notes.note: Regeneration is mild to moderate, never marked, despite severe anaemia [R2][R3]. The marrow is hypercellular, not hypoplastic [R1]. Pancytopenia is not a feature of the South African studies; leukocytosis with a left shift is more common [R1][R3].

Leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and pancytopenia are common at presentation and usually resolve within about 2 weeks of imidocarb [R5][R6]. Reticulocytosis appears by day 14 in most dogs [R4][R5]. In one dog, the counts took 5 months to return to normal [R24].

Pancytopenia was frequent in one Indian referral clinic [R9]. Non-regenerative anaemia was the entry criterion of the darbepoetin study [R18]. Parasite products delay reticulocyte maturation in vitro [R17].
One splenectomised dog developed haemophagocytic syndrome and needed immunosuppression [R10].

criteria.threshold: ARC below 60 x10^9/L in an anaemic dog
criteria.note: Cut-off used in B. rossi [R3] and in B. gibsoni (below 60 000/µL with haematocrit below 0.30 L/L) [R18]. A B. canis study used below 65 x10^9/L [R4]. Interpret with the days of illness.

criteria.threshold: ARC above the reference interval but below 150 x10^9/L
criteria.note: Used in the B. rossi marrow study, with a laboratory upper limit of 115 x10^9/L [R1].

criteria.criterion: Time before regeneration can be judged
criteria.threshold: 4 to 8 days after the onset of anaemia
criteria.note: General haematology figure quoted in the B. rossi marrow study; late samples (10 to 14 days) can also mislead [R1]. In B. rossi the ARC rose by day 3 of treatment [R3].

criteria.threshold: Anaemia, neutropenia or leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia together (below the laboratory reference intervals)
criteria.note: Definition used in B. canis and B. gibsoni case series [R6][R5]. Bicytopenia is two lines low [R6].

criteria.threshold: Bicytopenia or pancytopenia, and more than 2% haemophagocytic macrophages in the marrow aspirate
criteria.note: Criteria from a series of dogs of any cause [R11]. The B. vulpes case used 3% or more macrophages with phagocytosis of several cell lines [R10].

clinical_signs.note: Signs of the anaemia and the acute infection, not specific to a marrow problem [R4].
Uncommon in babesiosis; a bleeding tendency suggests chronic E. canis or theileriosis [R15][R16].

clinical_signs.sign: Fever, icterus, hepatomegaly or splenomegaly with persistent cytopenias
clinical_signs.note: Signs reported in haemophagocytic syndrome in dogs [R11].

clinical_signs.sign: Anaemia that persists or returns after antibabesial treatment
clinical_signs.note: Reason for referral in the B. vulpes case with haemophagocytic syndrome [R10].

tests.test: CBC with blood smear and manual reticulocyte count
tests.finding: Low ARC for the haematocrit; normocytic normochromic anaemia is usual [R3].
tests.note: A new methylene blue manual count does not stain Babesia; fluorescent analysers can overcount reticulocytes [R13][R12].

tests.finding: Rising ARC by day 3 to 6 in B. rossi [R3] and by day 14 in B. canis [R4].
tests.note: A rise confirms that the marrow responds; persistent cytopenias need further work-up [R5].

tests.test: PCR for Babesia species and for E. canis, Anaplasma and Theileria
tests.finding: Identifies the species and any co-infection.
tests.note: Co-infection was rare in B. rossi in the Eastern Cape [R14]; Theileria can cause anaemia and thrombocytopenia in South African dogs [R16].

tests.finding: Negative in the B. rossi marrow study [R1] and in the B. vulpes haemophagocytic case [R10].
tests.note: A positive test points to secondary IMHA (SY02).

tests.test: Bone marrow aspirate and core biopsy
tests.finding: B. rossi: hypercellular, erythroid dysplasia, increased iron and macrophages [R1]. Haemophagocytic syndrome: macrophages engulfing blood cells [R10]. Theileria: myelofibrosis [R16]. Chronic E. canis: hypoplasia [R15].
tests.note: Referral test. Take both aspirate and core [R11].

tests.finding: Both were raised in the B. vulpes dog with haemophagocytic syndrome [R10].
tests.note: Single case; no threshold in dogs with babesiosis.

differentials.distinguish: Fewer than 4 days of anaemia; ARC rises on repeat sampling [R1][R3].
Automated ARC higher than the manual count, no polychromasia, abnormal reticulocyte dot plot [R13][R12].
Bicytopenia or pancytopenia with marrow hypoplasia, bleeding and hypoalbuminaemia; positive E. canis serology or PCR [R15].
Theileria PCR positive, Babesia PCR negative; bleeding tendency; myelofibrosis on core biopsy in two dogs [R16].
Spherocytes, agglutination or positive Coombs test; usually a stronger reticulocyte response than babesiosis at the same haematocrit [R2].
Immune-mediated, neoplastic or idiopathic causes occur; marrow cytology and the response to treating the infection help [R11].
Megakaryocytes are adequate or increased in the marrow of B. rossi dogs [R1].

grading.criteria: 1 point for mild, 2 for moderate and 3 for marked anaemia, thrombocytopenia and leukopenia; 3 extra points for pancytopenia; 1 point for leukocytosis. A research score, not validated for treatment decisions [R5][R7].

approach.detail: CBC, smear and a manual reticulocyte count. Record how many days the dog has been ill. Do not call it non-regenerative before about 4 days of anaemia [R1][R13].

approach.action: Treat the infection and the anaemia
approach.detail: Give the antibabesial drug (TX00). Transfuse by the criteria in SY01. Transfusion corrected the anaemia but did not change the white cell or platelet response [R3].
PCR for E. canis, Anaplasma and Theileria, above all when cytopenias are marked, there is bleeding, or the dog is from an E. canis area [R14][R15][R16].
At day 3 to 6, and again at about day 14. Most dogs regenerate and their cytopenias resolve in this time [R3][R4][R5].
If cytopenias persist after effective treatment, or anaemia stays non-regenerative, refer for a bone marrow aspirate and core biopsy [R10][R11][R16].
Haemophagocytic syndrome: immunosuppression with continued antiprotozoal treatment, under specialist care [R10]. Co-infection: treat it (doxycycline for E. canis) [R23].

treatments.name: Antibabesial treatment alone
treatments.aim: Remove the parasite so that the marrow response and the blood counts recover.
treatments.evidence_summary: In 86 dogs with B. rossi treated with diminazene, the ARC rose by day 3 [R3]. In 22 dogs with B. canis, anaemia was corrected and the ARC was high 14 days after imidocarb [R4]. In 23 dogs with B. canis, cytopenias improved by about day 15 and all survived; 6 of 19 anaemic dogs never showed reticulocytosis [R5]. One B. canis dog with pancytopenia took 5 months to normalise [R24]. Drugs and doses are in TX00.
treatments.cautions: No source gives a dose change for dogs with cytopenias. See TX00 for the drug cautions.
treatments.monitoring: CBC and ARC at day 3 to 6 and at about day 14 [R3][R4][R5].

treatments.name: Packed red cell or whole blood transfusion
treatments.aim: Correct severe anaemia while the marrow response develops.
treatments.evidence_summary: In B. rossi, 32 transfused dogs were followed with 54 non-transfused dogs for 6 days. Transfusion corrected the anaemia but had no effect on white cell or platelet counts [R3]. The haematocrit rose more slowly in transfused dogs [R3]. Doses and triggers are in SY01.
treatments.cautions: A transfusion makes the next ARC harder to read [R3].

treatments.name: Doxycycline for E. canis co-infection
treatments.aim: Treat a concurrent E. canis infection that can cause pancytopenia and marrow hypoplasia.
treatments.evidence_summary: No study tested doxycycline for cytopenias in dogs with babesiosis. In 6 dogs infected with E. canis through ticks, a 20-day course cleared PCR at day 28, but 5 dogs became positive again; after a 28-day course, 4 of 5 stayed negative for 3 months [R23]. Evidence from E. canis alone, not babesiosis. Co-infection was rare in B. rossi in the Eastern Cape [R14].

doses.context: E. canis, 6 experimentally infected dogs, South African trial
doses.note: Actual doses given were 10 to 11.7 mg/kg. A 20-day first course was followed by relapse in 5 of 6 dogs.

treatments.cautions: Dogs with chronic E. canis and marrow hypoplasia all died in one series, whatever the treatment [R15].
treatments.monitoring: PCR after the course; the study tested at day 28 and later [R23].

treatments.name: Filgrastim (recombinant G-CSF)
treatments.aim: Raise the neutrophil and white cell count in pancytopenic dogs.
treatments.evidence_summary: Retrospective comparison in 20 pancytopenic dogs with B. gibsoni in India, all on doxycycline, clindamycin and metronidazole. The 10 dogs given filgrastim had a higher white cell count on day 7; 3 of 10 dogs without filgrastim died, and none with it [R9]. Groups were not randomised. Not tested in B. rossi or B. canis.

doses.context: B. gibsoni, 20 pancytopenic dogs, retrospective group comparison
doses.note: The paper is not consistent on the number of doses. Filgrastim is a human product.

treatments.cautions: No adverse effects were reported in the study, which did not look for them systematically [R9].
treatments.monitoring: White cell count; the study measured it on day 7 and day 28 [R9].

treatments.name: N-acetylcysteine
treatments.aim: Reduce oxidative injury and support recovery of red cells and platelets.
treatments.evidence_summary: In 32 pancytopenic dogs with haemoprotozoan disease (Babesia or Ehrlichia, species not reported by group), NAC with standard treatment gave higher haemoglobin and platelets at day 14 than standard treatment alone [R20]. In two small randomised trials in B. gibsoni (24 and 12 dogs), NAC gave faster recovery from anaemia [R21][R22]. The B. gibsoni trials did not select dogs with marrow failure.

doses.context: Pancytopenic dogs with Babesia or Ehrlichia, 32 dogs, controlled study
doses.note: Dose translated from a rat model by body surface area. The discussion says 14 days.

doses.context: B. gibsoni, 24 dogs, randomised pilot trial

treatments.cautions: The three studies are small, from India, and do not report adverse effects in the parts read [R20][R21][R22].
treatments.monitoring: CBC at day 14 to 28, as in the studies [R20][R21].

treatments.name: Immunosuppression for haemophagocytic syndrome
treatments.aim: Stop macrophage destruction of blood cells when haemophagocytic syndrome is confirmed.
treatments.evidence_summary: One splenectomised dog with B. vulpes and haemophagocytic syndrome received two immunosuppressive drugs, combined antiprotozoal drugs and three more transfusions. Platelets recovered quickly and the anaemia improved 10 days later; treatment was stopped without relapse [R10]. The drugs and doses are not in the abstract.
treatments.cautions: One group of authors warns that glucocorticoids predispose to secondary infection and gastrointestinal bleeding in haemoprotozoan disease [R20]. For immune-mediated haemolysis, see SY02.
treatments.monitoring: CBC and Babesia PCR until negative [R10].

treatments.name: Darbepoetin alfa
treatments.aim: Stimulate red cell production in non-regenerative anaemia.
treatments.evidence_summary: In 20 dogs with B. gibsoni and non-regenerative anaemia, 10 received clindamycin and doxycycline for 3 weeks and 10 received the same plus darbepoetin. Both groups were in clinical remission within 10 days; haematology did not differ [R18]. Serum erythropoietin was already raised in most dogs with babesiosis [R19], and the B. rossi marrow was hypercellular [R1].

doses.note: Dose used in the trial that found no benefit; not a recommendation.

prognosis.text: Cytopenias at presentation do not by themselves mean a poor outcome. In B. canis, 39 of 46 dogs survived [R6], and all 23 dogs of another study survived, with most cytopenias improved by day 15 [R5]. In B. rossi, regeneration usually begins within days of treatment [R3]. The outlook is poor when the marrow is hypoplastic from chronic E. canis [R15].

indicators.meaning: The marrow is responding; expected course [R3][R4].

indicators.finding: Persistent pancytopenia with marrow hypoplasia and E. canis
indicators.meaning: All 19 dogs in one series of chronic ehrlichiosis died [R15].

indicators.finding: Haemophagocytic syndrome with an infectious cause
indicators.meaning: Better 1-month survival than immune-mediated or idiopathic haemophagocytic syndrome [R11].

indicators.finding: Pancytopenia in B. gibsoni on triple therapy alone
indicators.meaning: 3 of 10 dogs died in one series [R9].

related.why: The antibabesial drugs and their doses.
Regenerative haemolytic anaemia and transfusion criteria and doses.
Secondary immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia and immunosuppression.
Leukopenia as a SIRS criterion and the order of care.

evidence_gaps: No study sampled the marrow of surviving dogs, or of dogs with B. canis or B. gibsoni; the only marrow study is of six fatal B. rossi cases.
No study tested antibiotic cover for neutropenic dogs with babesiosis; no source was found.
How much pancytopenia comes from co-infection with E. canis or Leishmania is unknown outside the Eastern Cape study.
No threshold of days after which a low ARC in babesiosis means true marrow failure was published.
The filgrastim and N-acetylcysteine studies are small, from India, and in B. gibsoni or mixed infections; none was done in B. rossi.
No dose of immunosuppressive drugs for haemophagocytic syndrome in babesiosis was found.

search.note: Local review (combined_set, disorder terms, article notes and full texts), PubMed searches for babesiosis with pancytopenia, bone marrow, non-regenerative anaemia, haemophagocytic syndrome and each candidate treatment, and web searches for co-infection treatment. The ACVIM ehrlichiosis consensus could not be opened (HTTP 403) and is not cited. Single case reports of cerebral or co-infected dogs with pancytopenia were left out.
